The p-value is one of the most misunderstood quantities in psychological research (Cohen 1994). Even professional researchers misinterpret it, and it is not unusual for such misinterpretations to appear in statistics textbooks!
The most common misinterpretation is that the p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true—that the sample result occurred by chance. For example, a misguided researcher might say that because the p-value is .02, there is only a 2% chance that the result is due to chance and a 98% chance that it reflects a real pattern in the population. But this is incorrect. The p-value is really the probability of a result at least as extreme as the sample result if the null hypothesis were true. So a p-value of .02 means that if the null hypothesis were true, a sample result this extreme would occur only 2% of the time.
You can avoid this misunderstanding by remembering that the p-value is not the probability that any particular hypothesis is true or false. Instead, it is the probability of obtaining the sample result if the null hypothesis were true.



Recall that null hypothesis testing involves answering the question, “If the null hypothesis were true, what is the probability of a sample result as extreme as this one?” In other words, “What is the p-value?” It can be helpful to see that the answer to this question depends on just two considerations: the strength of pattern in the sample and the size of the sample. Going back to our pigeons, if 10 out of 10 pigeons got the answers correct, that is a strong pattern. But it also depends on the sample size as you’ve seen in Figure 4, where even a small difference from chance (just 40 more pigeons than chance) is statistically significant when the sample size is large (1000 pigeons). That is, for the same difference (4% difference from chance) has a lower p-value when the sample size is larger. If only 54 out of 100 pigeons got the answers correct, although it’s the same 4% difference from chance, p-value is higher because the sample size is smaller. Bringing this to Psychological Science, let’s imagine a study in which a sample of 500 women is compared with a sample of 500 men in terms of hapiness on a scale 1 to 5. Hypothetically, let’s just say women were 2 points happier than men. If there were really no gender difference in the population, then that big of a difference in such a large sample should seem highly unlikely. Now imagine a similar study in which a sample of three women is compared with a sample of three men. Even if there were no gender difference in the population, 2-point difference in happiness based on such a small sample should seem likely. And this is precisely why the null hypothesis would be rejected in the first example and cannot be rejected in the second.
What you can remember from these examples is that weak patterns in small samples (N < 30) are not going to be statistically significant and that strong patterns based on larger samples (say, N > 100) are going to be statistically significant. If you keep this lesson in mind, you will often know whether a result is statistically significant based on the descriptive statistics alone. It is extremely useful to be able to develop this kind of intuitive judgment. One reason is that it allows you to develop expectations about how your formal null hypothesis tests are going to come out, which in turn allows you to detect problems in your analyses. For example, if your sample relationship is strong and you have a large enough sample, then you would expect to reject the null hypothesis. If for some reason your formal null hypothesis test indicates otherwise, then you need to double-check your computations and interpretations. A second reason is that the ability to make this kind of intuitive judgment is an indication that you understand the basic logic of this approach in addition to being able to do the computations.




A statistically significant result is not necessarily a strong one. Even a very weak result can be statistically significant if it is based on a large enough sample. This is closely related to Janet Shibley Hyde’s argument about gender differences [Hyde (2007). The differences between women and men in mathematical problem solving and leadership ability are statistically significant. But the word significant can cause people to interpret these differences as strong and important—perhaps even important enough to influence the college courses they take or even who they vote for. As we have seen, however, these statistically significant differences are actually quite weak—perhaps even “trivial.”1
This is why it is important to distinguish between the statistical significance of a result and the practical significance of that result. Practical significance refers to the importance or usefulness of the result in some real-world context. Many gender differences are statistically significant—and may even be interesting for purely scientific reasons—but they are not practically significant. In clinical practice, this same concept is often referred to as “clinical significance.” For example, a study on a new treatment for social phobia might show that it produces a statistically significant positive effect. Yet this effect still might not be strong enough to justify the time, effort, and other costs of putting it into practice—especially if easier and cheaper treatments that work almost as well already exist. Although statistically significant, this result would be said to lack practical or clinical significance.





The logic of null hypothesis significance testing (NHST) is to determine whether an observed pattern in a sample is likely to have occurred by chance or reflects a real pattern in the population.
The p-value is the probability of a sample result at least as extreme as the one observed under the null hypothesis.
The \(\alpha\)-level is the threshold for determining whether a p-value is low enough to reject the null hypothesis. By convention, it is set to .05. This is the Type I error rate that you will overclaim an effect when there is none.
A statistically significant result is one that has a p-value less than or equal to the \(\alpha\)-level, and passed the “is the observed pattern any different from chance?” question.
A statistically significant tells you that the pattern is different from chance, but it does not tell you by how much. A practically significant results are those that are strong enough to be useful in some real-world context.

title: Ch 5. Hypothesis Testing
text:
Imagine pigeons that can answer any Yes or No question by pecking. If someone claimed that that they created a new genetic line of magical pigeons who knew the answer to Yes or No questions, how would you put it to the test? When you ask just one of the pigeons whether a coin in your hand is showing heads or tails, and the pigeon gets it right, you would probably not be very surprised. After all, there is a 50% chance of getting the answer right even if the pigeon was just guessing. But what if you asked 4 pigeons and they all got it right? 10 out of 10 pigeons? If 10 out of 10 pigeons answered the questions correctly, you would probably be surprised and think that it is unlikely that the pigeons were just guessing. When would you be willing to believe that this new line of pigeons was indeed special and better than a luck would explain?


This is the exact logic of hypothesis testing that we will learn about in this chapter. Every pattern in your data can be interpreted in either of these two ways: It might have occurred by chance, or it might reflect some interesting pattern of the thing you are studying (in this case, the pigeons). So you need a way to decide between them. The general logic is as follows:

Assume, for the moment, that the pigeons are not special at all. Then, you can calculate the probability of a certain number of pigeons being correct just by guessing.
Determine how likely the observed pattern in your data would be if the pigeons were not special. In other words, how likely is it 10 pigeons would be correct just by chance?
If the observed pattern would be extremely unlikely, then you cannot hold the assumption that the pigeons are just guessing and would conclude that there are something interesting going on in these pigeons. If the pattern is within the range of what is likely to happen just by chance, there is not enough evidence to say that the pigeons are special.



You may have notice that the logic of answering “is the pattern real?” is mainly about “how likely is this pattern to occur by chance?” It turns out, we have a way to calculate how likely it is expected to occur by chance when you ask a certain number of pigeons. It is pretty intuitive that the probability of one pigeon getting a question correct by chance is 50% (assuming that half of your questions should be answered with Yes, the other half No). This is shown in Figure 1 with the bar highlighted in orange. Similarly, the probability of 2 out of 2 pigeons being correct by chance is 1/4, the probability of 4 out of 4 pigeons being correct by chance is 1/16 (Figure 2), and so on. The probability of all 10 pigeons being correct by chance is miniscule (Figure 3).


You can start by asking a question to just one pigeon in this new line of allegedly specialpigeons. Because the pigeon you chose belongs to the population of magical pigeons (i.e., a sample), you expect it to show some interesting power to answer a question correctly.
There are only two possible outcomes: the pigeon either gets it correct or incorrect. Figure 1 shows the probability of each outcome. The bar highlighted in orange shows the probability of the pigeon getting the answer correct by chance, which is 50%. The other bar shows the probability of the pigeon getting the answer incorrect by chance, which is also 50%. You can see that if you add up the probabilities of all possible outcomes, they sum up to 1.








Figure 1: How likely is it for this many pigeons to be correct by chance if a pigeon is just guessing? The bar corresponding to all pigeons getting answers correct is highlighted in orange. Probabilities are shown in Table 1.

Now, there are five possible outcomes: 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4 pigeons could get the answer correct. Figure 2 shows the probability of each outcome. This probability distribution is what math tells you, but empirically, you could also figure this out by keep asking four pigeons and noting how many got the answers correct. If you repeated this many times, you would see a distribution of outcomes that looks like Figure 2. The bar highlighted in orange shows the probability of all four pigeons getting the answer correct by chance, which is 6.25%. Again, if you add up the probabilities of all possible outcomes, they sum up to 1. Now you can notice that there is a mode in the distribution, and it is a symmetric distribution around the mode. There is some central tendency emerging – the distribution is clumped around the chance level of 50% correct. But this 6.25% chance is not low enough for you to decide that these pigeons are special. So you continue.

In this scenario, when did you decide that the result was not due to chance? How many pigeons would need to answer a question correctly before you would be willing to believe that this type of pigeon is indeed special? Some of you may have said that you would believe that the pigeons are special if 4 out of 4 pigeons got it right, while others may have said that you would not believe that the pigeons are special unless 10 out of 10 pigeons got it right. What was enough for you?
This decision depends on how sure you want to be. Let’s say you decided to believe that these pigeons were special after seeing 4 out of 4 pigeons were correct. However, there is still 6.25% chance that these pigeons could be correct just by guessing. As you make a decision to believe that these pigeon are special, you are taking a risk of making an error and believing this effect when there is none – in this case, 6.25% chance of making an error.
If you want to be more sure, you could ask 10 pigeons, and only believe that they are special if all of them are correct (Figure 3). You are being a lot more conservative, because the probability of all 10 pigeons being correct by chance is only about 0.098%.
There is an actual statistical test that formalizes this logic, called a binomial test. The binomial test is a statistical test that allows you to determine whether the number of a binary event like a yes/no response in a series of trials is significantly different from what would be expected by chance. In the case of the magical pigeons, the binomial test would allow you to determine whether the number of pigeons that answered correctly is significantly greater than what would be expected by chance (i.e., 50% correct). And, as it happens, binomial tests are often used on pigeons in real research. For example, pigeons are excellent at classifying visual patterns into different categories, and binomial tests are often used as a part of the process of establishing that a pigeon actually possesses some visual skill/ability to make the discrimination, and is not simply getting lucky.




What you just asked is whether the pigeons are any better than chance. And they seem to be. Now, if one of these pigeons tells you that a defendant is guilty, would you trust their answer? If they are available commercially, should you care to buy one? Before you put all your trust in these special pigeons, you should also think about how much better they are than chance would have it. Are their magical power really strong so they would get every single question right, or is it a more modest effect where, they are only slightly better than chance?


Let’s illustrate this with an example. If you asked 1000 pigeons a question and 540 of them got it right. Are they any better than chance? Probably, because there is only a very small chance that 540 or more pigeons would get it right just by chance (Figure 4). With increasing sample size, it gets harder and harder to get any difference just by chance, and just 40 more pigeons than the chance level is extremely unlikely in this scenario. So you say that these pigeons are indeed special and better than what luck would explain.








Figure 4: Number of Correct Pigeons Out of 1000 Pigeons. The bars corresponding to 540 or more pigeons getting answers correct is highlighted in orange.





How much better are they? Would you trust these pigeons to make a judgment about a defendant’s guilt? Maybe not, because they are only slightly better than chance (54% vs. 50%). Before you make any practical decisions based on the these pigeons who are outperforming chance, you should consider how much better they are than chance.

title: Ch 5. Hypothesis Testing
text:
What we have just considered with magical pigeons is exactly the logic of Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST), which is a formal approach to deciding between two interpretations of an observed pattern in a sample. One interpretation is called the null hypothesis (often symbolized \(H_0\) and read as “H-naught”). This is the idea that there is no such pattern in the population and that the observed pattern in the sample “occurred by chance.” The other interpretation is called the alternative hypothesis (often symbolized as \(H_1\)). This is the idea that there is indeed the same pattern in the population and that the observed pattern in the sample reflects this pattern in the population.


Again, every pattern in a sample can be interpreted in either of these two ways: It might have occurred by chance, or it might reflect a pattern in the population. So researchers need a way to decide between them. Although there are many specific null hypothesis testing techniques, they are all based on the same general logic. The steps are as follows:

Assume, for the moment, that the null hypothesis is true. In the population, there is no interesting pattern like the one observed in the sample.
Determine how likely the observed pattern in the sample would be if the null hypothesis were true.
If the observed pattern would be extremely unlikely, then reject the null hypothesis in favor of the alternative hypothesis. If it would not be extremely unlikely, then cannot reject the null hypothesis.

Following this logic, we can begin to understand why Mehl and his colleagues concluded that there is no difference in talkativeness between women and men in the population. In essence, they asked the following question: “If there were no difference in the population, how likely is it that we would find a difference of 546 words in our sample?” Their answer to this question was that a difference of 546 words (or, more precisely, a difference of this magnitude or extreme) would be fairly likely if the null hypothesis were true. Therefore, they failed to reject the null hypothesis—concluding that there is no evidence of a gender difference in the population.
Let’s unpack the second step of the logic a little more. Notice that their question, “If there were no difference in the population (the null hypothesis), how likely is it that we would find a difference of 546 words in our sample?”, has a if-then structure: If the null hypothesis about the population is true, then in our sample of the population, how likely is it that we would see a pattern like the one we observed in our sample? “If the null hypothesis were true” is a little bit of a mouthful, so we will often shorten it to “under the null” or “given the null.”
Because the sample is a subset of the population, if there something is true of the population, we should expect to see a similar pattern in our sample most of the time. However, sometimes, just by chance, the pattern in the sample may look very different from the population. For example, even if the pigeons were just guessers, if you keep probing 10 pigeons and noting how many got the answers right, a few of those “studies” will have 10 correct by chance (Figure 3). Similarly, imagine conducting a study like Mehl’s 100 times and lining up all 100 study results from smallest difference to largest gender difference. If men and women are equally talkative, most results cluster near no difference. Our observed difference of 546 words sits somewhere along this line. The question becomes, how many of those 100 studies found a difference at least as large as ours? If very few did, our result is unusual. It sits far out in the tail of the distribution of differences. This is the key idea of null hypothesis testing: the probability of the pattern at least as extreme as our sample or more extreme, under the assumption that there is no pattern in the population (the null hypothesis). Because this is such a central idea, it has a special name: the p-value. A low p-value means that the sample or more extreme result would be unlikely if the null hypothesis were true and leads to the rejection of the null hypothesis. A p-value that is not low means that the sample or more extreme result would be likely if the null hypothesis were true, and there is not enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis.
So how do we go from here to the binary yes/no answer to “Is this pattern real?” This is the question of deciding a threshold: how low the p-value must be for the sample result is considered unlikely enough to reject the null hypothesis. In null hypothesis testing, this threshold is called \(\alpha\) (alpha) level. By convention, the \(\alpha\)-level is almost always set to .05. If there is a 5% chance or less of a result at least as extreme as the sample result if the null hypothesis were true, then the null hypothesis is rejected. When this happens, the result is said to be statistically significant. If there is greater than a 5% chance of a result as extreme as the sample result when the null hypothesis is true, then the null hypothesis cannot be rejected. This does not necessarily mean that the researcher accepts the null hypothesis as true. It only means that there is not currently enough evidence to reject it. Researchers never use the expression “accept the null hypothesis.” or “the null hypothesis is true.”
As we discussed with the pigeon example, this decision comes with a risk of making an error. If you claim that there is an effect when there is none, you are making an error. This type of error is called a Type I error (Table 4). The \(\alpha\)-level is the probability of making a Type I error (Type I error rate). If you set the \(\alpha\)-level to .05, you are willing to take a 5% chance risk of making a Type I error. If you set the \(\alpha\)-level to .01, then you are accepting a 1% chance of making a Type I error.
However, there is also an error associated with being too conservative. Like many things in life, there is a trade-off in your decision. The problem with being too conservative is that you might be missing an interesting effect when there is one. This type of error is called a Type II error. Are you able to detect an effect when there is one? In other words, what’s the chance that you will NOT make a Type II error if there is indeed an effect? This is called the statistcal power. Power is simply our ability to correctly detect an effect that exists. It is influenced by the size of the effect (larger effects are easier to detect), the significance level we set (making it easier to reject the null makes it easier to detect an effect, but increases the likelihood of a Type I error), and the sample size used (larger samples make it easier to reject the null).



Table 4: Type I and II Errors






 You conclude …





“Statistically significant”
“Not statistically significant”


In reality, effect exists in the population.
Correct.
Type II Error.
False Negative.


In reality, no effect in the population. Just a fluke.
Type I Error.
False Positive. You overclaimed.
Correct.








The p-value is one of the most misunderstood quantities in psychological research (Cohen 1994). Even professional researchers misinterpret it, and it is not unusual for such misinterpretations to appear in statistics textbooks!
The most common misinterpretation is that the p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true—that the sample result occurred by chance. For example, a misguided researcher might say that because the p-value is .02, there is only a 2% chance that the result is due to chance and a 98% chance that it reflects a real pattern in the population. But this is incorrect. The p-value is really the probability of a result at least as extreme as the sample result if the null hypothesis were true. So a p-value of .02 means that if the null hypothesis were true, a sample result this extreme would occur only 2% of the time.
You can avoid this misunderstanding by remembering that the p-value is not the probability that any particular hypothesis is true or false. Instead, it is the probability of obtaining the sample result if the null hypothesis were true.



Recall that null hypothesis testing involves answering the question, “If the null hypothesis were true, what is the probability of a sample result as extreme as this one?” In other words, “What is the p-value?” It can be helpful to see that the answer to this question depends on just two considerations: the strength of pattern in the sample and the size of the sample. Going back to our pigeons, if 10 out of 10 pigeons got the answers correct, that is a strong pattern. But it also depends on the sample size as you’ve seen in Figure 4, where even a small difference from chance (just 40 more pigeons than chance) is statistically significant when the sample size is large (1000 pigeons). That is, for the same difference (4% difference from chance) has a lower p-value when the sample size is larger. If only 54 out of 100 pigeons got the answers correct, although it’s the same 4% difference from chance, p-value is higher because the sample size is smaller. Bringing this to Psychological Science, let’s imagine a study in which a sample of 500 women is compared with a sample of 500 men in terms of hapiness on a scale 1 to 5. Hypothetically, let’s just say women were 2 points happier than men. If there were really no gender difference in the population, then that big of a difference in such a large sample should seem highly unlikely. Now imagine a similar study in which a sample of three women is compared with a sample of three men. Even if there were no gender difference in the population, 2-point difference in happiness based on such a small sample should seem likely. And this is precisely why the null hypothesis would be rejected in the first example and cannot be rejected in the second.
What you can remember from these examples is that weak patterns in small samples (N < 30) are not going to be statistically significant and that strong patterns based on larger samples (say, N > 100) are going to be statistically significant. If you keep this lesson in mind, you will often know whether a result is statistically significant based on the descriptive statistics alone. It is extremely useful to be able to develop this kind of intuitive judgment. One reason is that it allows you to develop expectations about how your formal null hypothesis tests are going to come out, which in turn allows you to detect problems in your analyses. For example, if your sample relationship is strong and you have a large enough sample, then you would expect to reject the null hypothesis. If for some reason your formal null hypothesis test indicates otherwise, then you need to double-check your computations and interpretations. A second reason is that the ability to make this kind of intuitive judgment is an indication that you understand the basic logic of this approach in addition to being able to do the computations.




A statistically significant result is not necessarily a strong one. Even a very weak result can be statistically significant if it is based on a large enough sample. This is closely related to Janet Shibley Hyde’s argument about gender differences [Hyde (2007). The differences between women and men in mathematical problem solving and leadership ability are statistically significant. But the word significant can cause people to interpret these differences as strong and important—perhaps even important enough to influence the college courses they take or even who they vote for. As we have seen, however, these statistically significant differences are actually quite weak—perhaps even “trivial.”1
This is why it is important to distinguish between the statistical significance of a result and the practical significance of that result. Practical significance refers to the importance or usefulness of the result in some real-world context. Many gender differences are statistically significant—and may even be interesting for purely scientific reasons—but they are not practically significant. In clinical practice, this same concept is often referred to as “clinical significance.” For example, a study on a new treatment for social phobia might show that it produces a statistically significant positive effect. Yet this effect still might not be strong enough to justify the time, effort, and other costs of putting it into practice—especially if easier and cheaper treatments that work almost as well already exist. Although statistically significant, this result would be said to lack practical or clinical significance.

title: Ch.7: One Sample z-test and t-test
text:
Now that you have mastered the basic process of hypothesis testing, you are ready for this: your first real statistical test. The first question we can answer with hypothesis testing is whether a sample mean is significantly different from a baseline value. To answer this question, we can use either a one-sample z-test or a one-sample t-test.
Both one-sample z-tests and one-sample t-tests are used to determine whether a sample mean is significantly different from a baseline value. When do we use which? In a one-sample z-test, that baseline is some known population mean, and we also know the spread of the scores in the population (i.e., population standard deviation). In a one-sample t-test, the baseline can be a known population mean or a hypothesized value, but the spread of the scores is unknown, so we estimate it from the sample.
The logic is the same from before. We see something interesting in our data – in this case, the mean difference from the baseline value – and we want to know if that difference is “real” (statistical significance) and big enough to care (practical significance). For statistical significance, we start with the null hypothesis that there is no difference in the population, and we calculate the probability of observing sample means as extreme as the one we observed or more extreme if the null hypothesis is true. If that probability is low enough (lower than our threshold of significance, alpha), the data is unlikely enough under the null hypothesis that we conclude that there is something interesting going on in the population. For practical significance, we consider how large the difference between someone with the sample and someone with the baseline value.

title: Ch.7: One Sample z-test and t-test
text:
1 One-Sample z-Test
First, we need to formulate the research and null hypotheses. Remember, in such a hypothesis test, we are trying to compare two populations. Population 1, the research population, is the one from which we have drawn a research sample.






Figure 1: One-sample z-test by Nichole Vittoz



We do not have access to the actual research population mean, hence the need to calculate a sample mean. That sample mean is our best proxy for the population 1 mean, which we need to compare to the mean of population 2. The nature of the comparison, in particular its directionality, is determined by the researcher’s prediction.
Next, we need to determine what sample means we can expect if the null hypothesis is true. This distribution of sample means under the null hypothesis is shown in Figure 2. If the population mean is the same in both populations, then the sampling distribution of sample means will be centered on the population 2’s mean. The spread of the sampling distribution is determined by the standard error of the mean (SEM), which is the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size.








Figure 2: Distribution of Sample Means Under the Null Hypothesis






1.1 Margin of Error and Confidence Intervals
Our point estimate for the population mean is the sample mean, but Figure 2 shows that there is some uncertainty in what sample means we may observe when we only get to observe a subset of the true population, due to sampling error. As we’ve seen before, how far a sample mean can fall from the population mean with some confidence level is called the margin of error Figure 3. Confidence intervals communicate uncertainty with some degree of confidence by extending sample mean by the margin of error equally in both directions.
\[\text{Confidence Interval} = \text{Sample Mean} \pm \text{Margin of Error}\]








Figure 3: Margin of Error







1.2 Null Hypothesis and Alternative Hypothesis
The hypothesis that an apparent effect is due to chance is called the null hypothesis, written \(H_0\) (“H-naught”). The null hypothesis (H0) states that there is no significant difference between the sample mean and the baseline value. Subscript 0 will mark the parameters associated with the null hypothesis, so \(\mu_{0}\) indicates the population mean under the null hypothesis.
\[H_0 \colon \mu_{M} = \mu_{0}\]
The alternative hypothesis (\(H_1\)) needs to include all possibilities that are not included in the null hypothesis, because when the sample data is unlikely under the null hypothesis, we have to support the alternative hypothesis. The alternative hypothesis states that there is a significant difference between the sample mean and the baseline value.

1.2.1 Two-tailed Test
The simplest is the two-tailed test with non-directional hypothesis. It just states that the sample mean is not the same as the baseline value.
\[H_1 \colon \mu_{M} \neq \mu_{0}\]
What this is saying is that the difference can go either way – the sample mean can be either greater than or less than the baseline value. In this case, we need to distribute our Type I error rate \(\alpha\) equally across both tails (marked red in Figure 4). If the sample means are too low (outside of the cutoff valueson the left tail) or too high (on the right tail), then they are unlikely under the null hypothesis, and we reject the null hypothesis.








Figure 4: Two-Tailed Test. The sample means outside the cutoff values are unlikely under the null hypothesis. The area outside the cutoff values in both tails adds up to the significance level α (set to 0.05 in this example).







1.2.2 One-tailed Test
If the researcher has a directional hypothesis, and the population of interest can have only one directional difference from the baseline value, then a one-tailed test is appropriate. For example, if you are testing the mean height of 6-year-old children against the 5-year old baseline, it is reasonable to believe that, compared to the mean height of 5-year-olds, the mean height of 6-year-olds will be either the same (the null hypothesis) or greater (the alternative hypothesis). In this case, we can use a one-tailed test with a directional hypothesis.
\[H_1 \colon \mu_{M} > \mu_{0}\]
The Type I error rate is not split across two tails, but instead is concentrated in one tail (marked red in Figure 5). If the sample mean is too high (outside of the cutoff value on the right tail), then it is unlikely under the null hypothesis, and we reject the null hypothesis.
The same logic applies if the alternative hypothesis is that the sample mean is less than the baseline value, in which case the cutoff value is on the left tail.
\[H_1 \colon \mu_{M} < \mu_{0}\]












(a) \(H_1 \colon \mu \gt \mu_0\)













(b) \(H_1 \colon \mu \lt \mu_0\)







Figure 5: One-Tailed Test. The sample mean is unlikely under the null hypothesis. The area outside the cutoff value is shaded in red.







1.3 How Unlikely Are Sample Means as Extreme as the One Observed or More Extreme?
Now, we need to determine how unlikely the sample mean is under the null hypothesis: the p-value. We can find the probability in the tails of the sampling distribution using the z distribution. In Figure 6, the probability of observing a sample mean as extreme as the one observed or more extreme if the null hypothesis is true is represented by the shaded area in orange in both tails. If that probability is lower than our threshold of significance, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is a significant difference between the sample mean and the baseline value.








Figure 6: Two-Tailed Hypothesis Test. The sample mean M is outside of the cutoff values, and therefore unlikely under the null hypothesis. The p-value is the probability of observing a sample mean as extreme as M or more extreme if H0 is true. The shaded area in orange in both tails represents the p-value.






1.3.1 z Distribution Under the Hood
How did we find the p value? We used what we know about the standard normal distribution. We can standardize the sampling distribution of sample means by subtracting the population mean and dividing by the standard error of the mean. This gives us a z distribution, which is a standard normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. As noted before, the z distribution allows us to find probabilities for any sample mean under the null hypothesis.
Figure 7 shows the z distribution, which is the same as the sampling distribution of sample means, but standardized. The population mean under the null hypothesis is marked by a vertical line at 0, and the standard error of the mean is marked by a horizontal line extending from the center. Now, our unit is the standard error of the mean (i.e., z=1 is one standard error away from the population mean under the null hypothesis).








Figure 7: z Distribution





Figure 8 shows the same hypothesis test as Figure 6, but in terms of the z distribution. The observed sample mean is standardized to a test statistic z, which is the number of standard errors that the sample mean is away from the population mean under the null hypothesis. The p value is still the probability of observing a test statistic as extreme as z or more extreme if \(H_0\) is true.








Figure 8: Two-Tailed Hypothesis Test Using Test Statistic (z). test statistic z is outside of the critical values for z, and therefore unlikely under the null hypothesis. The p-value is the probability of observing a test statistic as extreme as z or more extreme if H0 is true. The shaded area in orange in both tails represents the p-value.








1.4 Statistical Significance Conclusion
Because the p-value is less than the significance level \(\alpha\) (i.e., the observed sample mean is unlikely enough under the null hypothesis), we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is a significant difference between the sample mean and the baseline value.


1.5 Big Enough Difference to Matter?
When we reject the null hypothesis, we are stating that the difference we found was statistically significant, but we have mentioned several times that this tells us nothing about practical significance. To get an idea of the actual size of what we found, we can compute a new statistic called an effect size. Effect size gives us an idea of how large, important, or meaningful a statistically significant effect is. For mean differences like we calculated here, our effect size is Cohen’s d:
\[d = \frac{M - \mu_{0}}{\sigma}\]
Essentially, we are comparing the difference between the sample mean and the population mean under the null hypothesis to the population standard deviation Figure 9.








Figure 9: Effect Size (Cohen’s d) for a z-test. The effect size is the standardized difference between the sample mean and the population mean under the null hypothesis. The effect size is calculated as d = (M - μ0) / σ.





Notice that this is very similar to our formula for z, but we no longer take into account the sample size (since overly large samples can make it too easy to reject the null). Cohen’s d is interpreted in units of standard deviations, just like z.
Cohen’s d is interpreted as small, moderate, or large. General guidelines suggest that d = 0.20 is small, d = 0.50 is moderate, and d = 0.80 is large Figure 10. Notice that as the effect size increases, the overlap between the individual scores under the null distribution (gray) and the population distribution (black) decreases. Obviously, values can fall in between these guidelines, so we should use our best judgment and the context of the problem to make our final interpretation of size.












(a) Small effect size (d = 0.2).













(b) Medium effect size (d = 0.5).













(c) Large effect size (d = 0.8).







Figure 10: Effect Size (Cohen’s d) Guidelines.




Effect sizes are incredibly useful and provide important information and clarification that overcomes some of the weakness of hypothesis testing. Any time you perform a hypothesis test, whether statistically significant or not, you should always calculate and report effect size.

title: Ch.7: One Sample z-test and t-test
text:
2 One-Sample t-Test
In reality, z-test is rarely used because we almost never know the population standard deviation. Instead, we use the sample standard deviation \(s\) to estimate the population standard deviation.






Figure 11: One-Sample t-Test by Nichole Vittoz



so our standard error of the mean becomes:
\[SEM = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
By doing this, however, we introduce more uncertainty into our estimate of the standard error of the mean. To account for this additional uncertainty, we use a different distribution called the t distribution to find probabilities for sample means under the null hypothesis.








Figure 12: t Distribution of Sample Means Under the Null Hypothesis





The t distributions are a series of distributions, based on the normal distribution, that adjust their shape according to degrees of freedom. The degrees of freedom for one-sample t-test is \(n - 1\), where \(n\) is the sample size. As the sample size increases, the degrees of freedom increase, and the t distribution approaches the z distribution.






Figure 13: Distributions Comparing Effects of Degrees of Freedom




2.1 Margin of Error and Confidence Intervals
Because t distribution is now used to find probabilities for sample means under the null hypothesis, our “confidence” also maps to different margin of error values. Our sample size not only determines the SEM, but also the critical values for t, \(t^*\).
\[\text{Margin of Error} = t^* \times \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
Confidence intervals are then calculated in the same way, by extending the sample mean by the margin of error in both directions.


2.2 Two-Tailed Hypothesis Test Using Test Statistic (t)
The logic of significance testing is the same as before. We are just finding the probabilities using the test statistic \(t\) instead of \(z\). The test statistic \(t\) is calculated as:
\[t = \frac{M - \mu_{0}}{SEM} = \frac{M - \mu_{0}}{s/\sqrt{n}}\]
We calculate the test statistic \(t\) and find the probability of observing test statistics as extreme as our \(t\) or more extreme if \(H_0\) is true. If this probability is less than our significance level \(\alpha\), we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is a significant difference between the sample mean and the baseline value (Figure 14).
This time, t is right outside of the critical values for t, and therefore still “unlikely enough” under the null hypothesis.








Figure 14: Two-Tailed Hypothesis Test Using Test Statistic (t). test statistic t is outside of the critical values for t, and therefore unlikely under the null hypothesis. The p-value is the probability of observing a test statistic as extreme as t or more extreme if H0 is true. The shaded area in orange in both tails represents the p-value.







2.3 Effect Size (Cohen’s d): Big Enough Difference to Matter?
The effect size, again, measures the standardized difference between the sample mean and the population mean under the null hypothesis. Because we do not know the population standard deviation, we use the sample standard deviation to calculate Cohen’s d for t-tests: \[d = \frac{M - \mu_0}{s}\]








Figure 15: Effect Size (Cohen’s d) for t-tests. The effect size is the standardized difference between the sample mean and the population mean under the null hypothesis. The effect size is calculated as d = (M - μ0) / s.







2.4 One-Sample t-Test Example
The personnel department for a major retail store in the Northeast reported that the average number of absences due to illness during the months of January and February for the past five years was equal to 7.85 days per employee. Assume the number of absences is normally distributed.
In an attempt to reduce absences, the company randomly selects 25 employees from multiple stores and offers them free flu shots this year. All 25 participants agree and the average number of absences in January and February for this sample was 6.25 days with SD = 3.15 days.
Do employees who receive flu shots have a different number of absences from the prior 5-year average (7.85)?

2.4.1 Confidence Interval
We will construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean number of absences in when flu shots are received.
\[\text{Margin of Error} = t^* \times \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
The critical value t depends on the degrees of freedom (\(df = n - 1 = 25 - 1 = 24\)) and the confidence level (95%). Using a t-table or statistical software, we find that the critical value \(t^*\) for \(df = 24\) and a two-tailed test at the 95% confidence level is approximately 2.064.
\[\text{Margin of Error} = 2.064 \times \frac{3.15}{\sqrt{25}} \approx 1.3\]
The standard error of the mean (SEM) is calculated as:
\[SEM = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{3.15}{\sqrt{25}} = 0.63\]
The 95% confidence interval for the mean number of absences when flu shots are received is:
\[95\% \text{ CI} = M \pm \text{Margin of Error} = 6.25 \pm 1.3 = [4.95, 7.55]\]
95% of the confidence intervals constructed the same was as this one would contain the true mean number of absences for employees who receive flu shots.


2.4.2 Hypotheses
Because it is conceivable that the flu shots could either increase or decrease absences (perhaps healthy employees are more likely to take time off), we will use a two-tailed test.

Null Hypothesis: People who receive flu shots have an average number of absences of is equal to the prior 5-yr average.

\[H_0: \mu_{\text{flu shot}} =7.86\]

Alternative Hypothesis: People who receive flu shots have an average number of absences of is equal to the prior 5-yr average.

\[H_1: \mu_{\text{flu shot}} \neq 7.86\]


2.4.3 Statistical Significance: How Unlikely is the Sample Mean (or More Extreme)?
To determine how unlikely the sample mean of 6.25 is (or more extreme) under the null hypothesis, we calculate the t-statistic:
\[t = \frac{M - \mu_{0}}{SEM} = \frac{6.25 - 7.85}{0.63} \approx -2.54\]
Note that t is negative because the sample mean is less than the population mean under the null hypothesis. However, because we are conducting a two-tailed test, we are interested in the absolute value of t.
With this statistic and t distribution, we can find the probability of observing a sample mean as extreme as 6.25 (or more extreme) if the null hypothesis is true. This is the p-value for our test.
\[p = 0.018\]








Figure 16: Two-Tailed Hypothesis Test Using Test Statistic (t). test statistic t is outside of the critical values for t, and therefore unlikely under the null hypothesis. The p-value is the probability of observing a test statistic as extreme as t or more extreme if H0 is true. The shaded area in orange in both tails represents the p-value.







2.4.4 Effect Size (Cohen’s d): Big Enough Difference to Matter?
The effect size, again, measures the standardized difference between the sample mean and the population mean under the null hypothesis. Because we do not know the population standard deviation, we use the sample standard deviation to calculate Cohen’s d for t-tests:
\[d = \frac{M - \mu_0}{s} = \frac{6.25 - 7.85}{3.15} \approx -0.51\]
According to Cohen’s guidelines, this is a medium effect size. Note that the effect size is a negative value, because the sample mean is less than the population mean under the null hypothesis. The magnitude of the effect size is what matters, not the sign.


2.4.5 Report the Results

One-sample t-test showed that the average number of absences for employees who received flu shots (M = 6.25, SD = 3.15) was significantly lower than the prior 5-year average of 7.85, \(t\)(24) = -2.54, \(p\) = 0.018, 95% CI = [4.95, 7.55]. The effect size was medium (Cohen’s d = -0.51). This suggests that receiving flu shots may have a meaningful impact on reducing employee absences during the months of January and February.

A few things to note about this example report:

Note that, although the test was two-tailed, you state that the sample mean was significantly lower than the baseline. If you just said that the sample mean was significantly different from the baseline, that’s not that informative.Readers may be left unsatisfied, wondering if the sample mean was higher or lower than the baseline. Reduce their cognitive load by telling them the direction of the difference.
\(t\), \(d\), and the direction should match:


If you say the sample mean is “lower” than the baseline, then \(t\) and \(d\) backing up that statement should be negative.
If you say the sample mean is “higher” than the baseline, then \(t\) and \(d\) backing up that statement should be positive.


Note that I did not elaborate the p-value as “the probability of observing sample means as extreme as 6.25 or more extreme if flu shots had no effect”. APA style lets us communicate all this information in a concise way by simply reporting (1) that you used a null hypothesis test (e.g., one-sample t-test), and (2) the p-value. The reader can then interpret the p-value in the context of the null hypothesis test. The same goes for the confidence interval. What this means for you as a reader is that you should be able to interpret and deciper \(p\) and \(CI\) values in the context of the null hypothesis test without needing to be told what they mean!
I reported the p value to three decimal places, which is standard practice. If the p-value is less than 0.001, you can report it as \(p < .001\). In the old days, it was common to just say \(p < .05\), but we want to give the readers more information than that so if they have a different threshold for significance, they can make their own decision about whether the result is significant or not.

When you observe some interesting pattern in your data, you might wonder whether it’s not just statistically real but also meaningful in practice. Effect size answers this by quantifying the strength of an effect in terms of the variability of the raw scores, independent of sample size, making it comparable across studies. You can assess this using standardized effect size metrics. The effect sizes in Table 8 all express an observed quantity relative to a reference unit, producing a value whose magnitude can be interpreted as small, medium, or large.

title: 1 Statistics Overview
text:
Footnotes


Standard Error of the Mean (SEM) is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean. Because the variance of a sum of independent values is the sum of their variances, the variance of the mean is the population variance divided by the sample size. The SEM is therefore the square root of that: the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size. When the population standard deviation is unknown, the sample standard deviation is used instead.↩︎

title: Lab 1: R Basics
text: In this lab, we will learn how to interact with R using R Rstudio. R is a programming language that you will write code in, and RStudio is a program that makes working with R easier. The user can either install R and RStudio on their computer and work with them locally or choose to work with them remotely via an internet browser. In this course, we will work with R and RStudio remotely via PositCloud.

title: Lab 1: R Basics
text:
Learning Objectives

Be familiarized with RStudio.
Be able to write and run code in the console.
Be able to create a new Markdown (Quarto) file, write code in it, and render the file to an html document.
Understand objects and functions in R.
Be able to load packages.
Be able to read in data.

title: Lab 1: R Basics
text:
1 Introduction to R and RStudio
As previously mentioned, R is a programming language that we will use to write code for working with data. RStudio is an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) for R. RStudio is dependent on R but separate from it. It provides a useful interface for working with R and has several advantages over the default R interface. Think of it as knowing English and using a plain text editor Notepad or TextEdit to write a book versus using a word processor like Microsoft Word. You could do it on a plain text editor, but it would be much harder without things like spell-checking and formatting and you wouldn’t be able to use some of the advanced features that Word has developed. In a similar way, you can use R without RStudio but we wouldn’t recommend it. RStudio serves as a text editor, file manager, spreadsheet viewer, and much more. The key thing to remember is that although you will do all of your work using RStudio for this course, you are actually working with two pieces of software, which means that from time to time, both of them may have separate updates.
RStudio runs on Mac, PC, and Linux machines and provides a simplified interface that looks and feels identical on all of them. While it can be installed on your own computer, for this course you will be asked to login to a shared RStudio Cloud server (PositCloud) from a web browser. There are several advantages to using the web browser application of RStudio Cloud. It allows you to write and access R code wherever you go. It even works on your tablet because it does not require installation. It also makes it much easier to collaborate with others, and since no installation is required, you can work on projects on any device as long as you are connected to the internet. Another significant advantage of using RStudio in the cloud is that you can run time-consuming scripts without bogging down your own device. However, because RStudio Cloud requires an internet connection, it will run slower if your internet connection is not fast or stable.

1.1 R Studio Panes
The interface for working with RStudio both in the cloud or locally is largely the same and consists of four main “panes” each in a quadrant of your screen. Several of the panes are further subdivided into multiple tabs.



R Studio Panes



1.1.1 Source Pane
By default, the upper left pane is the source pane, where you view, write, and edit code from files and view data tables in a spreadsheet format.


1.1.2 Console Pane
The lower left pane is the console pane, where you can view the output of your coding and computations. It is also possible to write code directly into the console. However, keep in mind that the code you write in the console will run and can create objects that will be saved in the environment, but the code itself won’t be saved. You need to write your code into a script or a Markdown/Quarto file in the source pane to save it.


1.1.3 Environment Pane
The right panes have several different tabs that show you information about your code. The most used tabs in the upper right pane is the Environment tab. The Environment tab lists some information about the objects that you have defined in your code.


1.1.4 Output Pane
In the lower right pane are tabs for browsing files, viewing plots, managing R packages, reading help files, and for viewing html documents and presentations. The most used tabs are the Files tab for directory structure.


1.1.5 Keyboard Shortcuts

F6 and Shift+F6 navigates focus between panes. To check which tab the focus is on, press Shift+Tab.
Ctrl+1 moves your cursor to the source pane.
Ctrl+2 moves your cursor to the console.

title: Lab 1: R Basics
text:
2 Writing R Code
R is a command based system. We type commands, R translates them into machine instructions, which our computer then executes, and then we often, but not necessarily, get back some output. The commands can be typed into the R console, or else they can be put into a script and run as a batch.

2.1 R Console
When learning R, it is usually best to start with typing commands in the R console. When we open RStudio initially, our console will usually look something like this:
R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24) -- "Happy Hop"
Copyright (C) 2026 The R Foundation for Statistical Computing
Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu

R is free software and comes with ABSOLUTELY NO WARRANTY.
You are welcome to redistribute it under certain conditions.
Type 'license()' or 'licence()' for distribution details.

R is a collaborative project with many contributors.
Type 'contributors()' for more information and
'citation()' on how to cite R or R packages in publications.

Type 'demo()' for some demos, 'help()' for on-line help, or
'help.start()' for an HTML browser interface to help.
Type 'q()' to quit R.

>
Notice that at the bottom, there is a single line beginning with >. This is the R console’s command prompt, and it is where we type our commands. We then press Enter, and our command is executed. The output of the command, if any, is displayed on the next line or lines, and then a new > prompt appears.
At the R console prompt (>), type 5 and press Enter. You will find the output [1] 5. The [1] at the beginning of the line indicates the index (the position) of the first element displayed on that specific line. Try running 1:50 in the console, where the colon operator (:) generates a sequence from 1 to 50. What’s useful to remember at this point is that outputs follow the index inside the square brackets [].

2.1.0.1 Keyboard Shortcuts

Ctrl+2 moves your cursor to the console prompt (>).
Ctrl+` moves your focus to the console output.

While R is much more than a simple calculator, a useful way to familiarize yourself with R and the console is to do some simple calculator-like computations. Most of this will work just like you would expect from a typical calculator.
For example, if you are curious what 5 plus 3 is, the inputs are 5 and 3, and the operation is addition You can express this as a simple R code. At the R console prompt (>), type 5+3 and press Enter. You will get 8.
Some basic math operators in R are listed here:

Math Operators and Symbols


Function
Symbols




Addition
+


Subtraction
-


Multiplication
*


Division
/ (forward slash)


Exponent
^









TipExercise 1



Find answer to the following questions using R console.

2026 plus 12
1 divided by 5
50 times 4
9 squared
170 minus 15






2.2 Quarto
This is a Quarto document which enables you to weave together formatted text, called Markdown, and executable code into a finished document. When you “render” this .qmd file, the code in the “code chunks” in this document will be executed (or more colloquially, “run”), and you will be able to see the output in an .html file. In fact, if you are reading this on the course website, you are reading the rendered HTML document.
There is a very similar type of document called R Markdown whose extension is .Rmd. They are essentially the same, except that “render” is called “knit” and it’s specialized for R only. Quarto is the next-generation successor to R Markdown. It has better accessibility features can support languages other than R. For that reason, we will be using Quarto in this course.

2.2.1 Markdown (formatted text)
The markdown space in an .qmd file is ideal for writing notes that explain your analysis and document your thought process. Effectively documenting your work in the markdown space enhances both the clarity and reproducibility of your analysis.
Headings are useful in organizing the outlines. The hashtag # marks the heading level, where # is heading level 1, ## is heading level 2, and so forth.
Lists can be created using * or -. For example,

Item 1
Item 2

You will find other formatting examples throughout this Quarto document.


2.2.2 Code Chunks
Everything you write inside the code chunks will be interpreted as code and executed by R. Code chunks start with three backticks and an r tag (```{r}), followed by some space for your code, and end with another three backticks (```). If you accidentally delete one of those backticks, your code won’t run and/or your text parts will be interpreted as part of the code chunks or vice versa.
You can embed code like this.

31^2

[1] 961


You can insert a new code chunk in several ways:

Click the Insert a new code chunk button in the RStudio Toolbar (green icon at the top right corner of the Source pane).
Select Code > Insert Chunk from the menu.
Using the keyboard shortcut Ctrl + Alt + I for Windows or Cmd + Option + I on a Mac.
Type ```{r} and ``` manually.



2.2.3 (Optional Note) YAML header
You might have noticed that this .qmd file starts with a block fenced with three dashes ---.
title: "Lab 1. R Basics"
author:
 - "Yeon Soon Shin"
 - "Anjali Thapar"
 - "Gaby Mahrholz"
 - "Carolina E. Kuepper-Tetzel"
format: 
  html:
    html-math-method: plain
You don’t need to worry about the syntax of this at this point, but if you are curious, this block specifies metadata for the document. For example, the title of the document is “Lab 1. R Basics” and the document should be rendered as an html file.


2.2.4 Rendering Quarto
When you render this file, a document will be generated that includes both content and the output of embedded code. To render, you can use the following options:

Graphic User Interface

Click on the Render button in the RStudio Toolbar (blue right arrow icon at the top of the source pane).

Using the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+K.
Using Console

Navigate to the console (Ctrl+2).
Run library(quarto) to import quarto library. You need to do this only once when you start the session.
To render an html file from Quarto, type the command quarto_render("lab01-r-basics.qmd")
To open the result html file, type the command browseURL("lab01-r-basics.html")








Caution



Note that you need to allow pop-up window from your browser to successfully open the rendered html file.


This will open a new tab with an html file that contains the output. You can repeat this step to run all code chunks in this file. This is generally a good practice because you will want to make sure that the code runs cleanly from top to bottom.
Note that if you have already rendered the file and a tab is open on your browser, it may look like nothing happens when you render. Go find the open tab called matches the title (here, Lab 1. R Basics). The tab is refreshed when you render.






TipExercise 2



Render this Quarto document to an html file. Inspect an output of the code chunk above. What is the output?




2.2.5 Creating and Saving a New Quarto File

Select File > New File > R Script from the menu.
When the file is open, save the file. You can save the file by the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on a Mac.
Choose the file name with an .qmd extension (e.g., lab01-LASTNAME.qmd). A popup will ask you “Are you sure you want to change the type of the file so that it is no longer an R script?”. Select Yes.







TipExercise 3



Create a new Quarto file, add a code chunk with some math operations, save it, and render it.

title: Lab 1: R Basics
text:
3 Objects and Functions in R

3.1 Object (Variable)
You can also store the output as an “Object” (or a variable), so you can reuse them. For example, you might want to store the output of 3 + 5 operation as an object x and do different things with it. To assign 3 + 5 to the object x, you write the object on the left of the = sign, and the value on the right.
Type x = 3 + 5 in the console and press Enter. Nothing will happen in the console output. However, if you type x again in the console, it will give you the output 8, indicating that the output of the 3+5 operation is stored in the object x.
Alternatively, you can use <- to assign values to an object, which makes it clear that output of the operation on the right side should be assigned to (hence the arrow) the left side. You can repeat the above steps with y <- 3 + 5.
Now, you can use the object y to do different things with it. For example, you can multiply y by 2. Without writing (3+5)*2, you can pass the output of 3+5 to the next operation *2.






TipExercise 4



Store the output of 10*2 in an object z and divide z by 4.




3.2 Functions
R has some nice basic functions (a set of operations put together), also written as objects. Function objects need a parenthesis () so you can pass the input to the function. For example, if you want an object with different numbers in it, you can use a function c() where c stands for concatenate.

x <- c(1,3,2,4,3,3,4,2,5)
x

[1] 1 3 2 4 3 3 4 2 5


Again, you can do other things with this object x, such as taking the mean of the numbers in it. There is a function mean() that calculates the mean for you.

mean(x)

[1] 3








TipExercise 5



In your new Quarto document, add a code chunk, and get the square root of 5329 using a function sqrt(). Render the document to find the output.

title: Lab 1: R Basics
text:
4 Installing and Loading Packages
When you install R you will have access to a range of functions including options for data wrangling and statistical analysis. The functions that are included in the default installation are typically referred to as “base R” and you can think of them like the default apps that come pre-loaded on your phone. One of the great things about R, however, is that it is user extensible: anyone can create a new package that extends its functionality. There are currently thousands of packages that R users have created to solve many different kinds of problems, or just simply to have fun. For example, there are packages for data visualization, machine learning, interactive dashboards, web scraping, and playing games such as Sudoku. Packages are not distributed with base R, but have to be downloaded and installed from an archive. The main repository where packages reside is called CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network.
There is an important distinction between installing a package and loading a package.

4.0.1 Installing Packages with install.packages()
When you install R and RStudio for the first time (or after an update), most of the packages we will be using won’t be pre-installed. Before you can load new packages like, you will need to install them.
If you try to load a package that has not been installed yet, you will receive an error message. To fix this, simply install the package first. This is done using the function install.packages(). For example, if you wnat to install package called tidyverse, you can run install.packages("tidyverse"). This only needs to be done once after a fresh installation. After that, you will be able to load the tidyverse package into your library whenever you open RStudio.
For this course, most of the packages we will be using are pre-installed.


4.0.2 Loading packages with library()
This is like launching an app on your phone: the functionality is only there when the app is launched and remains there until you close the app or restart RStudio.

library(tidyverse)  # for data wrangling

── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

library(gt)         # for pretty tables

The hashtag (#) marks everything to the right of it as comment. Using comments can be very useful for annotating your code, and it improves the readability too. It will also help you to remember why/what you done months later, when you return to your code that you have inevitably forgotten!

title: Lab 2: Measurement Reliability
text:
In this lab, we will explore the concepts of measurement reliability. Measurement is a critical aspect of empirical research, and it is the foundation for drawing valid conclusions from data. Measurement reliability is important if we want to compare one measurement to another, because the relationship between two different variables can’t be any stronger than the relationship between either of the variables and itself (i.e., its reliability). This means that an unreliable measure can never have a strong statistical relationship with any other measure. For this reason, researchers developing a new measurement (such as a new survey) will often go to great lengths to establish and improve its reliability.
This lab will use Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (Rosenberg 1965) to demonstrate how to assess reliability of measurement.

title: Lab 2: Measurement Reliability
text:
Learning Objectives

Understand the concepts of reliability in measurement.
Produce a scatter plot to visualize the relationship between two items in a scale.
Calculate Cronbach’s α to assess internal consistency of a scale.
Calculate composite scores for a scale.
Interpret what the results of reliability mean in the context of research.
Write up the results of reliability analyses in the APA style.

title: Lab 2: Measurement Reliability
text:
3 Reliability (internal consistency)
Good measurement is reliable, and the measurement of the same construct should produce similar results across different items (internal consistency), different time points (test-retest reliability), or different raters (inter-rater reliability).
In today’s lab, we will focus on internal consistency. Let’s say we want to measure Self-Esteem. What we want to obtain from our measurement is some score that represents Self-Esteem for an individual. But we don’t just ask one question “Do you have high self-esteem?” for many reasons. For one, increasing the amount of data helps us be more accurate and more confident in our measurement. People may make mistakes when answering a single question and can be influenced by other things outside of the question itself (maybe they are distracted by notifications on their phones). To guard against this, we ask multiple questions that are supposed to measure the same construct. For example, in RSES, we ask multiple questions that measure self-esteem: “I feel that I am a person of worth, at least on an equal plane with others.” (Item 1) and “All in all, I am inclined to feel that I am a failure.” (Item 3). If someone has high self-esteem, they will strongly agree with the first statement and strongly disagree with the second statement. If someone has low self-esteem, they will strongly agree with both statements. But what if someone strongly agrees with both statements? Then we have a problem, and the scale is not reliable to use.
To summarize, we want to check if the items are internally consistent and correlated with each other. We will first inspect pairs of items, and then quantify overall internal consistency of the scale.

3.1 Inspect pairs of items

3.1.1 Scatter plots
We will first create a scatter plot of the items to visually inspect their relationships. If the items are internally consistent, we should see a pattern of positive correlation between them. As we discussed above, Items 1 and 3 are supposed to measure the same construct, but they are worded in opposite directions. Therefore, we expect to see a negative correlation between these two items. We will create a scatter plot of Items 1 and 3 to visualize their relationship.
For this, we will use ggplot() function from the ggplot2 package to create a scatter plot. We will map the first item (RSES01) to the x-axis and the third item (RSES03) to the y-axis. So what do we do with the mapped data? We need to specify what else needs to happen with that data. For ggplot(), we keep adding layers to the plot using + operator. For example, we can add a layer to the plot that adds points to the plot using geom_point() function. We can also add a layer that adds a regression line to the plot using geom_smooth() function.
Since the responses are on a 4-point Likert scale, we will use geom_jitter() to add some random noise to the points so that we can see the distribution of the responses more clearly.

# create a scatter plot of the items
df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RSES01, 
             y = RSES03)) + # map the first item to the x-axis and the third item to the y-axis
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2, height = 0.2) + # add some random noise to the points so individual dots are visible
  labs(x = "Item 1", # add label to the x-axis
       y = "Item 3", # add label to the y-axis
       title = "Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale") + # add title to the plot
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1) + # make the x and y axes have the same ratio
  theme_classic() # use a classic theme for the plot








This chart has title 'Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale'.
It has x-axis 'Item 1' with labels 0, 1, 2 and 3.
It has y-axis 'Item 3' with labels 0, 1, 2 and 3.
The chart is a set of 318 big solid circle points of which about 86% can be seen.
It has alpha set to 0.5.




3.1.2 Correlation coefficient
We see a bunch of dots, but we would like to quantify the trend in the data. We can do this by calculating the correlation coefficient between the two items.
What’s the correlation between the two items? We can calculate the correlation using cor() function. To look at a specific variable (column) in a data frame, we can use the $ operator. For example, to look at the first item (RSES01), we can use df$RSES01. To look at the third item (RSES03), we can use df$RSES03. We can then pass these two variables to the cor() function to calculate the correlation between them. Think of this cor() function as something like the sqrt() function that we used in Lab 1. The sqrt() function takes a number as input and returns the square root of that number. Similarly, the cor() function takes two variables as input and returns the correlation between them.

# calculate the correlation between the two items
cor(df$RSES01, df$RSES03)

[1] -0.5262346








NoteRounding Numbers



If the number you got is a little too long and have many decimal places, you can round the number to 3 decimal places using round() function. For example, if you want to round the correlation to 3 decimal places, you can use round(cor(df$RSES01, df$RSES03), 3). Alternatively, you can use the pipe operator %>% to pass the output of cor() function to round() function. For example, cor(df$RSES01, df$RSES03) %>% round(3).








TipExercise 1




Choose two items from RSES that are expected to be positively correlated and create a scatter plot of the two items. Report the correlation between the two items. Are the two items positively correlated? If not, what could be the reason?
Choose two items from RSES that are expected to be negatively correlated and create a scatter plot of the two items. Report the correlation between the two items. Are the two items negatively correlated? If not, what could be the reason?






3.2 Quantify overall internal consistency with Cronbach’s α
We use Cronbach’s α (read as “Cronbach’s alpha”) to quantify the internal consistency. If Cronbach’s α is greater than or equal to 0.7, we can say that the items are internally consistent and reliable. Ideally, we want to see Cronbach’s α to be greater than 0.8, but this is not always the case in practice.
We will create an array of keys, where the items that need to be reverse scored are prefixed with a minus sign (-). For example, for the third item “All in all, I am inclined to feel that I am a failure.”, we will use -3 to indicate that this third item needs to be reverse scored.
For this example, we will only look at the first five items.

rses.keys <- list(RSES = c(1, 2, -3, 4, -5))







NoteList



This is a data structure called a list. A list is a collection of objects that can be of different types. What is important to note here is that we can specify a name for each element in the list (in this case, RSES is the name of the first element in the list). We can access the elements in the list using the $ operator. For example, to access the first element in the list, we can use rses.keys$RSES. This will return a vector of numbers that represent the items in RSES that need to be scored.

rses.keys

$RSES
[1]  1  2 -3  4 -5



rses.keys$RSES

[1]  1  2 -3  4 -5




With the keys defined, we can now score the items in RSES using scoreItems() function from the psych package. This function will calculate the composite scores and also calculate Cronbach’s α for the scale.

# score the items in RSES (columns that start with "RSES") using the keys defined above
rses <- scoreItems(
  keys = rses.keys, 
  items = df %>% select(starts_with("RSES")),
  totals = TRUE
)







NoteFunction With Named Arguments



So far, the functions that we took one or two inputs. For example, cor() function takes two inputs (two variables) and round() function takes two inputs (a number and the number of decimal places to round to). However, some functions can take multiple inputs. For example, scoreItems() function takes three inputs: keys, items, and totals. The first input is the keys that we defined above, the second input is the items in RSES that we want to score, and the third input is a logical value that indicates whether we want to calculate the total scores for each participant. In this case, we set totals = TRUE to calculate the total scores for each participant.
When you specify the input arguments with their names (e.g., keys = rses.keys), it is called named arguments. This is useful when a function takes multiple inputs, and you want to specify which input corresponds to which argument. If you don’t specify the names of the arguments, the function will assume that the inputs are in the order that they are defined in the function. If you don’t specify the names of the arguments, you can still use the function, but it is less readable and more prone to errors. For example, if you want to use scoreItems() function without named arguments, you can achieve the same result as above with the following code:

rses <- scoreItems(rses.keys, df %>% select(starts_with("RSES")), TRUE)

It is less readable because you have to remember the order of the arguments, and it is more prone to errors because you can easily mix up the order of the arguments. Therefore, it is a good practice to use named arguments when a function takes multiple inputs.



3.2.1 Composite scores
You can find the RSES scores for each participant under scores in the rses object. $ operator is used to accuess the scores in the rses object. The scores is a data frame that contains the composite scores for each participant. We can convert the scores to a tibble for easier inspection.

# convert the scores to a tibble
rses.scores <- rses$scores %>% 
  as_tibble()

3.2.2 Internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha)
Now this is what we wanted to do all along. Let’s check internal consistency of the scale. For this, we will examine the Cronbach’s α for the RSES scale. We can access the Cronbach’s α values from the rses object.






TipQuestions to answer about the data:




Is the RSES scale internally consistent (Cronbach’s alpha >= 0.7)?




# check the Cronbach's alpha for the RSES scale
rses$alpha %>% 
    round(3) %>% # round the Cronbach's alpha to 3 decimal places
    knitr::kable()





RSES




alpha
