3.2.3 Write up the results
We will now write up the results of the reliability analysis. The reliability analysis is conducted to justify the use of a measure in research, and thus the results of reliability analysis is usually reported in the method section of a research paper, following the description of the measure:

We used the Revised Self-Esteem Scale (RSES) to measure self-esteem. RSES is a brief measure of self-esteem, with 10 items. Participants rated the extent to which they agreed with each statement on a 4-point Likert scale (0 = Strongly Disagree, 3 = Strongly Agree). Composite scores were calculated by summing the responses across the first five items with reverse scoring applied to the appropriate items (Items 3, 5).

Following this description, you would report the results of the reliability analysis. The write-up should include the purpose of the analysis (to assess internal consistency), the method used (Cronbach’s α), and the results of the analysis (the Cronbach’s α value), and the interpretation of the results (good, acceptable, or poor internal consistency). For example:

Reliability analysis using Cronbach’s α showed that the RSES had good internal consistency (α = .85).







TipReliability Analysis Write-Up Checklist




What type of reliability is measured? (e.g., internal consistency)
What method is used to assess reliability? (e.g., Cronbach’s α)
What are the results of the analysis? (e.g., Cronbach’s α values for the scale)
What is the interpretation of the results? (e.g., good? acceptable? poor?)









TipExercise 2



Repeat the reliability analysis for the RSES using all 10 items. Write up the results of the reliability analysis in APA style in your own words. You can use the example write-up above as a guide, but do not copy it verbatim. Make sure to include the description of the scale and how the score was calculated, the purpose of the analysis, the method used, the results of the analysis, and the interpretation of the results.





Key Takeaways

Internal consistency is a type of reliability that measures consistency of items within a scale, and it can be assessed using Cronbach’s α.
Cronbach’s α values greater than or equal to 0.7 indicate acceptable internal consistency, while values less than 0.7 indicate poor internal consistency.
scoreItems() function from the psych package can be used to calculate composite scores for a scale and also calculate Cronbach’s α.



3.3 Additional Notes






NoteAn Alternative Way to Calculate Composite Scores



Can you guess how you can calculate the composite scores without using scoreItems() function? If you thought about just adding up the scores for each item, then you are correct! For example, to calculate the composite scores for the first five items in RSES, you can use the following code, which should give you the same results as the scoreItems() function.

composite_scores <- df$RSES01 + df$RSES02 + (3 - df$RSES03) + df$RSES04 + (3 - df$RSES05)

head(composite_scores) %>%
  knitr::kable()




x

Note that we need to reverse score the appropriate items (Items 3 and 5) by subtracting the scores from 3. This is because the items are scored on a 4-point Likert scale (0-3), and we want to reverse the scoring for the items that are negatively worded.
If this feels like a lot of work, you can use the function scoreItems() from the psych package to do this for you. This function takes care of reverse scoring and calculating the composite scores for you. It also calculates Cronbach’s α for the scale, so that is a bonus! I just wanted to show you that you don’t need all these bells and whistles to calculate composite scores, but it is nice to have them when you are doing research.

title: Lab 3: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
This lab will orient you to the very first steps of data analysis. When you get a new dataset, it is important to take a quick look at the data before proceeding with any analysis and answer your research questions. This is called exploratory data analysis (EDA). EDA is a critical step in the data analysis process because it allows you to understand the structure of the data, identify any potential issues, and get a sense of the state of each variable. To conduct EDA, you will inspect if the raw data look right (no missing data, appropriate range of responses, etc.), and visualize the data to understand the shape of the distributions along with descriptive statistics.
You will work with survey data on sleep and breakfast consumption. We asked 59 Bi-Co students about how much sleep they get on average and how many days a week they eat breakfast, along with their demographic information on class year and home campus.
What kind of questions would you want to answer about this dataset? Before reading onto the answer, pause here to think about what you would want to know about this dataset.
With these questions in mind, let’s start exploring the data.

title: Lab 3: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
3 Univariate Analysis
Univariate analysis involves examining the distribution of each variable one at a time. With this, we are asking single-variable questions: what is the state of each variable? The answer to this question includes the typical response (central tendency) and how much variability there is in the responses (spread), and the shape of the distribution.
How we conduct univariate analysis depends on the type of variable. Table 1 shows different approaches to univariate analysis depending on the type of variable.



Table 1: Approach to univariate analysis based on the type of variable





Type of Variable
Approach to Univariate Analysis




Categorical, Ordinal
Frequency table, bar chart


Interval, Ratio
Histogram, box plot, descriptive statistics






In our dataset, we have one categorical variable (Campus), one ordinal variable (Class), and two ratio variables (SleepDuration, BreakfastPerWeek). We will conduct univariate analysis for each of these variables in the following sections.

3.1 Categorical Variable: Campus

3.1.1 Data Wrangling
The correct data type is important for conducting data analysis. The data type of the Campus variables should be factor, which has specific levels that represent the categories of the variable. The following code converts the Campus variables to factor data type, with two levels: “Bryn Mawr College” and “Haverford College”.
First, make sure that the values of the Campus variable are spelled correctly and match the expected categories. You can use unique() function to check the unique values of the Campus variable.

unique(df$Campus)

[1] "Bryn Mawr College" "Haverford College"


If this looks right, you can convert the Campus variable to factor data type using mutate() and factor() functions. The levels argument specifies the levels of the factor, and the ordered argument specifies whether the levels are ordered or not. In this case, we set ordered = FALSE because there is no inherent order to the categories of the Campus variable.
You can check if the data type of the Campus variable is factor and what the levels of the factor are using class() and unique() functions, respectively.

df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    Campus = factor(Campus, 
                    levels = c("Bryn Mawr College", 
                               "Haverford College"), 
                    ordered = FALSE),
  )

class(df$Campus)

[1] "factor"

unique(df$Campus)

[1] Bryn Mawr College Haverford College
Levels: Bryn Mawr College Haverford College

Do the levels of the factors match the expected categories?





3.1.2 Frequency Table
Frequency tables are a simple way to summarize categorical or ordinal variables. They show the number of observations and the percentage of observations in each category.






TipQuestions to answer about the data:

Which level is the most common (called mode)? Which level is the least common?



tabyl() function from the janitor package creates a frequency table. We can also add the total sample size using adorn_totals() and choose how many decimal places to display using adorn_pct_formatting(). Finally, we use kable() function from knitr to create a pretty table.

df %>% 
  tabyl(Campus) %>%
  adorn_totals("row") %>%
  adorn_pct_formatting(digits = 2) %>%

3.1.3 Bar Chart
For categorical and ordinal variables, bar charts are a good way to visualize the distribution of the variable. Bar chart has the same information as the frequency table, but it is easier to spot the most common response and the distribution of the responses.






TipQuestions to answer about the data:

The following code using geom_bar() of ggplot() creates a bar chart for the Campus variable.

df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Campus)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "count") +
  labs(x = "Campus", y = "Frequency") +

TipBar Chart Checklist




Are axes labeled correctly, where x-axis shows the levels of the variable and y-axis shows the frequency of each level?
Is the order of the levels informative (e.g., alphabetical order, or order of importance)?






3.2 Ordinal Variable: Class
For the Campus variable, it doesn’t matter whether the level looks like c("Bryn Mawr College", "Haverford College") or c("Haverford College", "Bryn Mawr College"), because there is no inherent order to the categories. However, for the Class variable, the order of the levels matters because it is an ordinal variable. The following code converts the Class variable as factor, with four levels: “First-year”, “Sophomore”, “Junior”, and “Senior”. The order of the levels is important because it reflects the natural order of the class years. You can achieve this by setting the ordered argument to TRUE in the factor() function.
Other than this, all the steps for univariate analysis of the Class variable are the same as those for the Campus variable. You can create a frequency table and a bar chart for the Class variable using the same approach as for the Campus variable.

3.3 Ratio Variable: SleepDuration
SleepDuration is a ratio variable, which means it has a true zero point (e.g., 0 hour means you don’t get any sleep), and the intervals between values are meaningful. Another name for interval and ratio variables is continuous variables. For continuous variables, we can summarize the data using descriptive statistics: the central tendency (mean, median) and spread of the variable (standard deviation and range) and the shape of the distribution (skew and kurtosis). Mean and standard deviation are the most commonly used descriptive statistics, especially when the distribution of the variable is approximately normal. This makes it important for us to check if the responses are normally distributed.
We can do this by first visualizing the distribution of the variable using histograms and box plots, and run statistical tests to check for normality.

3.3.1 Descriptive Statistics
Descriptive statistics are a set of summary statistics that describe the central tendency, spread, and shape of the distribution of a variable. For instance, for sleep duration, we can summarize how much sleep Bi-Co students are getting on average, and how much variability there is in the amount of sleep they are getting.






TipQuestions to answer about the data:




Are there any missing values in the variable? If so, how many observations are missing?
What is the central tendency of the variable?
What is the spread of the variable?
What is the shape of the distribution of the variable?

Is the distribution approximately normal (bell-shaped, symmetric around one peak)? If not, which direction is the distribution skewed (positive or negative)?




The describe() function from the psych package provides a convenient way to calculate descriptive statistics for interval and ratio variables. The following code calculates descriptive statistics for the SleepDuration variable. We are specifically interested the two central tendency measures (mean and median), two spread measures (standard deviation sd and range), minimum min and maximum max values, and two shape measures (skew and kurtosis).

df %>% select(SleepDuration) %>%
  describe() %>%
  select(n, mean, median, sd, range, min, max, skew, kurtosis) %>%
  knitr::kable()

3.3.2 Histogram
As we did with the bar chart for categorical and ordinal variables, we can use a histogram to visualize the distribution of interval and ratio variables. The histogram makes the answers to our questions about the shape of the distribution more apparent.

The following code creates a histogram for the SleepDuration variable using geom_histogram() function of ggplot(). The binwidth argument specifies the width of the bins in the histogram. In this case, we set the binwidth to 1 hour, which means that each bin will represent 1 hour of sleep duration.

  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, color = "black", fill = "lightgray") +

This means that there are students who are getting extremely low amounts of sleep. In this case, the median is a better measure of central tendency than the mean, because the mean is vulnerable to extreme values.






TipHistogram Checklist

Is the binwidth appropriate for the variable? If not, adjust the binwidth and recreate the histogram.





3.3.3 Box plot
Box plots convey rich information about the distribution of a variable. It shows the central tendency and the spread of the distribution, as well as the presence of outliers.






TipQuestions to answer about the data:




What is the median sleep duration of the students?
What is the range that the middle 50% of the students fall into (interquartile range)?
What is the range of sleep duration among the students (excluding outliers)?
How many outliers are present in the box plot?
Is the distribution approximately normal and symmetric around the median? If not, which direction is the distribution skewed (positive or negative)?



Let’s first make a box plot for the SleepDuration variable. We can use geom_boxplot() function of ggplot() to create a box plot. The following code creates a box plot for the SleepDuration variable.

df %>% ggplot() +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x="",
                   y=SleepDuration)) +
  labs(y = "Sleep Duration (hours)", 
       x = "") +
  ggtitle("Sleep Duration")








This chart has title 'Sleep Duration'.
There is no x-axis.
It has y-axis 'Sleep Duration (hours)' with labels 4, 6, 8 and 10.
The chart is a boxplot comprised of 1 vertical box with whiskers.
There is a box at x=1.
It has median 7.5. The box goes from 7 to 8, and the whiskers extend to 6 and 9.
There are 1 max and 1 min outliers for this boxplot.


The center-line in the middle of the box shows the median of the distribution. The upper edge of the box is the third quartile (Q3; 75% of the cases fall at or below this value); the lower edge is the first quartile (Q1; 25% of the cases fall at or below this value), which makes the box to represent the middle 50% of the data. If the distribution is skewed, the distance between the center line and the upper versus lower edge of the box will not be the same. When there are no outliers, the whiskers (the line) extend to the lowest and the highest score in the distribution. Outliers are plotted as separate points. If one whisker is long relative to the other or if there are outliers on only one side of the distribution, the distribution will be skewed in that direction (positive skew for outliers above Q3; negative skew for outliers below Q1). These outliers are values that fall outside of 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR) from the first and third quartiles. For example, if the IQR is 1 hour (i.e., the range of the middle 50% of the students sleep is 1 hour), then any values that are more than 1.5 hours below Q1 or above Q3 will be considered outliers. title: Lab 3: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
text:
Key Takeaways

Visualizing data and the shape of the distribution is an important step in EDA.
The types of variables inform how to conduct EDA (Table 1).
If the distribution of a continuous variable is normal, mean and standard deviation are appropriate measures of central tendency and spread, respectively.
If the distribution is not normal, mean and standard deviation are not appropriate measures of central tendency and spread. For this reason, it is important to check the normality of the distribution using visualization (histogram).

title: Lab 4: Standard Scores and Probability
text: In this lab, we will practice finding standard scores from probability values and vice versa, and convert between raw scores and standard scores.

title: Lab 4: Standard Scores and Probability
text:
Learning Objectives

Convert between raw scores and standard scores (z scores).
Find probabilities from z scores and vice versa.







NoteBasic concepts to keep in mind:




The cutoff values are on the x-axis of the normal distribution curve.
The probability corresponds to the area under the curve.
The probability adds up to 1. The total area under the curve is 1.



How extraverted/introverted are you compared to the average person? To answer this question, we will use the Big Five Inventory (BFI) extraversion scale.
Respond to the following three items from the Big Five Inventory (BFI), on a scale of 1 to 5 (1 = strongly disagree and 5 = strongly agree). Take the mean of the three items to get a single composite score.

I see myself as someone who is talkative.
I see myself as someone who is reserved (Reverse).
I see myself as someone who is outgoing, sociable.

BFI extraversion has a mean of 3.48 and a standard deviation of 0.65. Given this information, are you more extraverted or introverted than the average person? By how much? Is that unusual?
If we assume that the scores are normally distributed, then we can find out exactly how unusual/special your score is, using the standard score (z score) and probability.

title: Lab 4: Standard Scores and Probability
section: 1 Going Between Raw Scores and z Scores
text:
1 Going Between Raw Scores and z Scores
Once we know the raw score and the mean and standard deviation, we can convert it to a z score or vice versa. Remember that R is just a fancy calculator, so we can find z scores and raw scores using the formulas we learned in class.
Say, we have a raw score of 2.67, and want to know the relative standing of that score in the unit of “typical” deviations (SD):

mean <- 3.48
sd <- 0.65
raw_score <- 2.67
z <- (raw_score - mean) / sd
z

[1] -1.246154


If you know the z score and want to find the raw score, you are just reversing that steps. If you know someone is 1.5 standard deviations above the mean, and you know the mean and the standard deviation, you can find the raw score using the formula:

mean <- 3.48
sd <- 0.65
z <- 1.5
raw_score <- z * sd + mean
raw_score

[1] 4.455








TipExercise 1



Use the formulas above to convert the following z scores to raw scores and vice versa:

z = -1.96, mean = 3.48, sd = 0.65
raw score = 9.18, mean = 12.26, sd = 1.57

title: Lab 4: Standard Scores and Probability
section: 2 Using R to Find z Scores and Probabilities
text:
2 Using R to Find z Scores and Probabilities
How extreme is your extraversion, given the population mean and standard deviation? In other words, what are the chances to see someone with your extraversion score or more extreme (on either end)? For this, we need to find the corresponding probability in the tail of your z score.
You can use the z Distribution app, or you can just use R to find the probability without all the bells and whistles. It is up to you which one you use. Here, I show you how to do it in R.
R provides functions to help us find standard scores and probabiilities. All of these functions assume that the probability is on the left side of the curve (lower tail), because the default is to calculate the cumulative probability from the bottom (left).

qnorm: find the standard score (z-score) for a given probability.
pnorm: find the probability for a given standard score (z-score).

These are anchors that will help us remember which function to use:

pnorm(0) # should return 0.5, because there is exactly half of the area below the mean (0)

[1] 0.5

qnorm(0.5) # should return 0, because the mean (center) is at 0

[1] 0

title: Lab 4: Standard Scores and Probability
text:
3 z Scores to Probability

3.1 Probability Below a z Score (Lower Tail)
Let’s start with a simple case. We want to know how much of the normally distributed data is below a z-score of −1. From the empirical 68-95-99.7 rule, we know that about 34% of the data is between the mean and -1, and about 50% of the data is below the mean. So we expect the probability to be about 50 - 34 = 16%. Let’s see what R says.

pnorm(-1)

[1] 0.1586553


That’s pretty close! But what if we want to know how much of the data is below a z score of, say, −1.2? There is no simple rule for that, so we will use R to get the corresponding probability.

pnorm(-1.2)

[1] 0.1150697








TipExercise 1



Find the probability below the following z-scores:

-2
-1.96
-1.645
-1.28
0





3.2 Probability Above a z Score (Upper Tail)
To find the probability above a z score, we can use the fact that the total area under the curve is 1. So, if we want to find the probability above a z score of −1, we can subtract the probability below that z score from 1.

1 - pnorm(-1)

[1] 0.8413447


The same goes for probabilities above any z score.

1 - pnorm(1)

[1] 0.1586553








TipExercise 2



Find the probability above the following z-scores:

2
1.96
1.645
1.28
0

Compare the values you get with the ones from Exercise 1. What do you notice?


Because the normal distribution is symmetric, the probability below a z score of −1 is the same as the probability above a z score of 1.


3.3 Probability in Both Tails
What if we want to find the probability outside of a z score of −1 and 1? We can find the probability below −1 and above 1, and add them together.

pnorm(-1) + (1 - pnorm(1)) 

[1] 0.3173105


Or, because of the symmetry, we can just find the probability below −1 and double it.

2 * pnorm(-1)

[1] 0.3173105


If you like working with positive numbers, you can get the same results by finding the probability in the top tail above 1 and doubling it.

2 * (1 - pnorm(1))

[1] 0.3173105


All of these methods will give you the same result.






TipExercise 3



Find the probability in both tails outside of the following z-scores:

-2 and 2
-1.96 and 1.96
-1.645 and 1.645
-1.28 and 1.28





3.4 Probability Between Two z Scores
The numbers don’t have to be symmetric. For example, we can find the probability between folks 1.5 standard deviations below the mean and 1 standard deviation above the mean. Because pnorm gives us the cumulative probability from the bottom, we can find the probability below z=1 and subtract the probability below z=-1.5.

pnorm(1) - pnorm(-1.5)

[1] 0.7745375








TipExercise 4



Find the probability between the following z-scores:

-1.645 and -0.524
-0.524 and 0.842
0.842 and 1.645

title: Lab 4: Standard Scores and Probability
text:
4 Probability to z Scores
Students find it a little more challenging to go from probability to z scores. But it is just the reverse of what we did above. We will use the qnorm function to find the z score for a given probability.

4.1 Probability Below a z Score (Lower Tail)
Let’s start with a simple case. We want to know what the corresponding standard score is for the bottom 1% of the normal distribution.

qnorm(0.01) 

[1] -2.326348


Let’s try a few more examples.






TipExercise 5



Find the z-scores below which the following percentages of the normal distribution fall:

2.275%
2.5%
5%
50%





4.2 Probability Above a z Score (Upper Tail)
Now, let’s find the z-scores above which 1% of the normal distribution falls. Because qnorm calculates the cumulative probability from the left, we need to express the probability in terms of the lower tail. Top 1% means that 99% from the bottom (100% - 1% = 99%).

qnorm(1 - 0.01)

[1] 2.326348








TipExercise 6



Find the z-scores above which the following percentages of the normal distribution fall:

2.275%
2.5%
5%
50%

Compare the values you get with the ones from Exercise 1. What do you notice?




4.3 Probability in Both Tails
What this means is that, when we want to find the z-scores where the probability outside of those z-scores is known, that’s just twice the probability in one tail. For example, if we want to find the z-scores where 1% of the distribution is outside of those z-scores in both tails (equal distance from the mean), we are essentially finding the z-scores where 0.5% is in the lower tail and 0.5% is in the upper tail.

qnorm(0.01 / 2) # lower tail

[1] -2.575829

qnorm(1 - 0.01 / 2) # upper tail

[1] 2.575829








TipExercise 7



Find the z-scores outside of which the following percentages of the normal distribution fall:

4.55%
5%
10%





4.4 Probability Between Two z Scores
What if we want to find the z-scores from bottom 10% to top 5%? They are not symmetric, so what do we do?
This is exactly what we did for finding the z-scores for the bottom 10% and the top 5%.

qnorm(0.95) # top 5 %

[1] 1.644854

qnorm(0.10) # bottom 10 %

[1] -1.281552








TipExercise 8



Find the cutoff z scores for the following probabilities:

Bottom 5% to Bottom 30%
Bottom 30% to Top 20%
Top 20% to Top 5%

title: Lab 4: Standard Scores and Probability
text:
5 Putting It All Together
z scores are just the bridge between raw scores and probabilities. If you want to find the probability from a raw score, you first convert the raw score to a z score, and then use that z score to find the probability. If you want to find the raw score from a probability, you first find the z score for that probability, and then convert that z score to a raw score.
Or better yet, you can use the pnorm and qnorm functions to do all of that in one step. For example, if you want to find the probability below a raw score of 120 when the mean is 100 and the standard deviation is 15, you can use pnorm to do that in one step:

pnorm(q=120, mean=100, sd=15)

[1] 0.9087888


For the reverse, the same idea applies. If you want to find the raw score below which 90% of the data falls, you can use qnorm to do that in one step:

qnorm(p=0.90, mean=100, sd=15)

[1] 119.2233


Using this, we can find the range of Big Five Inventory (BFI) scores that would correspond to the middle 95% of the population. The BFI has a mean of 3.48 and SD of 0.65. 95% is in the middle, so each tail has 2.5% of the data.

qnorm(p=0.025, mean=3.48, sd=0.65) # lower cutoff

[1] 2.206023

qnorm(p=1-0.025, mean=3.48, sd=0.65) # upper cutoff

[1] 4.753977


Writing numbers repeatedly is tedious and error prone, so we will store the numbers in variables and use those variables in the calculations.

m_bfi <- 3.48
sd_bfi <- 0.65
p_tail <- 0.025 # probability in each tail
lower_cutoff <- qnorm(p_tail, m_bfi, sd_bfi)
upper_cutoff <- qnorm(1-p_tail, m_bfi, sd_bfi)

95% of the population has BFI scores between 2.2060234 and 4.7539766. In another words, 5% of the population will have BFI scores more extreme than those cutoff scores. From this, you can already see if your extraversion score is outside of this range or now. But to find out the exact probability of seeing someone with your extraversion score or more extreme, we can use pnorm to find the probability.
For example, if you want to find the probability below a raw score of 2.5 (a score that’s below the mean), you can use pnorm to do that in one step:

pnorm(q=2.5, mean=3.48, sd=0.65)

[1] 0.06581665


If you want to find the probability above a raw score of 4.5 (a score that’s above the mean), you can just subtract the probability below that raw score from 1, as we practiced in Exercise 6.

1-pnorm(q=4.5, mean=3.48, sd=0.65)

[1] 0.05829709

title: Lab 5: One-Sample t-Test
text:
This lab is adapted from Kevin P. McIntyre’s OSL Open Stats Lab.

In this lab, we will conduct our first statistical test. Exciting!
Today’s data comes from Tworek and Cimpian (2016). Tworek and Cimpian (2016) investigated what predicts people’s tendency to think what “is” is what “ought to be”. They hypothesized that this tendency is related to people’s preference for explanations that are based on inherent properties (e.g., “Pink is the color associated with girls because of something about the color pink or about girls— maybe because pink’s flower-like appearance matches girls’ dainty nature”) versus extrinsic properties (e.g., “Pink is the color associated with girls because of some historical or contextual reason—maybe because businesses promoted pink products for girls over the last century.”)–called “inherence bias”.
For this lab, we will explore whether there is a significant inherence bias in the population, first answering a single-variable question: what is the state of the inherence bias in the population?
In their first study, Tworek and Cimpian (2016) recruited a sample of 122 adults on an online platform called Amazon Mechanical Turk. Inherence bias was measured using 15 items that asked participants to rate their agreement with inherence-based explanations on a 9-point scale (1 = disagree strongly, 9 = agree strongly). For example, participants were presented with a statement like “Pink is the color associated with girls because of something about the color pink or about girls— maybe because pink’s flower-like appearance matches girls’ dainty nature” and asked to rate their agreement with that statement on a 9-point scale. The composite score is the average of the 15 items. We want to test whether the average inherence bias score in the population is different from 5, which is the midpoint of the scale.
One-sample t-tests are perfect for this type of question – we have a single variable that we want to test against some baseline value, and we do not know the population standard deviation.


The null hypothesis is that the average inherence bias score in the population is equal to 5. The alternative hypothesis is that the average inherence bias score in the population is not equal to 5. Because the average inherence bias could be either higher than 5 (indicating that there is indeed an inherence bias in the population) or lower than 5 (indicating that people have bias in the opposite direction and find explanations in the extrinsic properties), we will conduct a two-sided test.
H0 : μ = 5 H1 : μ ≠ 5

TipStudy 2



Do you find the results from Study 1 convincing? For one, what if people just have a general tendency to agree with any statement, regardless of whether it is based on inherent or extrinsic properties? To address this concern, Tworek and Cimpian (2016) conducted a second study.

The relative preference score is the difference between the two scores (inherent - extrinsic). This difference score is in diff variable in the dataset. The baseline value is 0, which indicates no preference for either type of explanation.

title: Ch.8: Paired Samples t-test
text:
So far, we have dealt with data measured on a single variable at a single point in time, allowing us to gain an understanding of the logic and process behind statistics and hypothesis testing. Now, we will look at a slightly different type of data that has new information we couldn’t get at before: difference within individuals. Specifically, we will look at how the value of a variable, within people, changes across two time points, or differs across two conditions. This is a very powerful thing to do, and, as we will see shortly, it involves only a very slight addition to our existing process and does not change the mechanics of hypothesis testing or formulas at all!


Researchers are often interested in change over time. Sometimes we want to see if change occurs naturally, and other times we are hoping for change in response to some manipulation. In each of these cases, we measure a single variable at different times, and what we are looking for is whether or not we get the same score at Time 2 as we did at Time 1. The absolute value of our measurements does not matter—all that matters is the change, or the difference score. Let’s look at an example.



Table 1: Raw and difference scores before and after training

Table 1 shows scores on a quiz that five employees received before they took a training course and after they took the course. The difference between these scores (i.e., the score after minus the score before) represents improvement in the employees’ ability. The third column is what we look at when assessing whether our training was effective. We want to see positive scores, which indicate that the employees’ performance went up. What we are not interested in is how good they were before the training or after the training. Notice that the lowest-scoring employee before the training (with a score of 1) improved just as much as the highest scoring employee before the training (with a score of 8), regardless of how far apart they were to begin with. There’s also one improvement score of 0, meaning that the training did not help this employee. An important factor in this is that the participants received the same assessment at both time points. To calculate improvement or any other difference score, we must measure only a single variable.
When looking at change scores like the ones in Table 1, we calculate our difference scores by taking the Time 2 score and subtracting the Time 1 score. That is:
\[X_{D} = X_{T2} - X_{T1}\]
Where \(X_{D}\) is the difference score, \(X_{T1}\) is the score on the variable at Time 1, and \(X_{T2}\) is the score on the variable at Time 2. The difference score, \(X_D\), will be the data we use to test for improvement or change. We subtract Time 2 minus Time 1 for ease of interpretation; if scores get better, then the difference score will be positive. Similarly, if we’re measuring something like reaction time or depression symptoms that we are trying to reduce, then better outcomes (lower scores) will yield negative difference scores.
While we frequently use difference scores for data that are collected from the same participants twice, we can also test to see if people who are matched or paired in some way agree on a specific topic. These are called matched pairs data. For example, we can see if a parent and a child agree on the quality of home life, or we can see if two romantic partners agree on how serious and committed their relationship is. In these situations, we also subtract one score from the other to get a difference score. This time, however, it doesn’t matter which score we subtract from the other because what we are concerned with is the agreement.
In both of these types of data, what we have are multiple scores on a single variable. That is, a single observation or data point is comprised of two measurements that are put together into one difference score. This is what makes the analysis of change unique—our ability to link these measurements in a meaningful way. This type of analysis would not work if we had two separate samples of people that weren’t related at the individual level, such as samples of people from different states that we gathered independently.


It is important to point out that the paired samples t-test has been called many different things by many different people over the years: paired samples, related samples, matched pairs, repeated measures, dependent measures, dependent samples, and many others. What all of these names have in common is that they describe the analysis of two scores that are related in a systematic way within people or within pairs, which is what each of the datasets usable in this analysis have in common. As such, all of these names are equally appropriate, and the choice of which one to use comes down to preference. In this text, we will refer to paired samples, though the appearance of any of the other names throughout this chapter should not be taken to refer to a different analysis; they are all the same thing.
Now that we have an understanding of what difference scores are and know how to calculate them, we can use them to test hypotheses. As we will see, this works exactly the same way as testing hypotheses about one sample mean with a t statistic. The only difference is in the format of the null and alternative hypotheses.




When we work with difference scores, our research questions have to do with change. Did scores improve? Did symptoms get better? Did prevalence go up or down? Our hypotheses will reflect this. Remember that the null hypothesis is the idea that there is nothing interesting, notable, or impactful represented in our dataset. In a related samples t test, that takes the form of “no change.” There is no improvement in scores or decrease in symptoms. Thus, our null hypothesis is:
\[H_0: \text{There is no change or difference in the population.}\] \[H_0: \mu_D = 0\]
As with our other null hypotheses, we can express the null hypothesis for parired samples t-tests in both words and mathematical notation. The exact wording of the written-out version should be changed to match whatever research question we are addressing (e.g., “There is no change in ability scores after training”). However, the mathematical version of the null hypothesis is always exactly the same: the average change score is equal to zero. Our population parameter for the average is still \(\mu\), but it now has a subscript \(D\) to denote the fact that it is the average change score and not the average raw observation before or after our manipulation. Obviously, individual difference scores can go up or down, but the null hypothesis states that these positive or negative change values are just random chance and that the true average change score across all people is 0.
Our alternative hypotheses will also follow the same format that they did before: they can be directional if we suspect a change or difference in a specific direction, or we can use an inequality sign to test for any change:
Two-tailed test: \[H_1: \text{There is a change or difference in the population.}\] \[H_1: \mu_D \neq 0\]
One-tailed tests (improvement or increase): \[H_1: \text{The average score increases in the population.}\] \[H_1: \mu_D > 0\]
One-tailed tests (decline or decrease): \[H_1: \text{The average score decreases in the population.}\] \[H_1: \mu_D < 0\]
As before, your choice of which alternative hypothesis to use should be specified before you collect data based on your research question and any evidence you might have that would indicate a specific directional (or non-directional) change.





Our test statistic for the change scores follows exactly the same format as the one-sample t-test. In fact, the only difference is in the data that we use. For our change test, we first calculate a difference score as shown above. Then, we use those scores as the raw data in the same mean calculation, standard error formula, and t statistic. Let’s look at each of these.
The mean difference score is calculated in the same way as any other mean: sum each of the individual difference scores and divide by the sample size.
\[M_D = \frac{\sum X_D}{n}\]
Here we are using the subscript \(D\) to keep track of that fact that these are difference scores instead of raw scores; it has no actual effect on our calculation. Using this, we calculate the standard deviation of the difference scores the same way as well:
\[s_D = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (X_D - M_D)^2}{n - 1}} = \sqrt{\frac{SS}{df}}\]
Once we have our standard deviation, we can find the standard error:
\[SEM = \frac{s_D}{\sqrt{n}}\]
Finally, our test statistic t has the same structure as well:
\[t = \frac{M_D - \mu_D}{SEM} = \frac{M_D - \mu_D}{s_D/\sqrt{n}}\]
As we can see, once we calculate our difference scores from our raw measurements, everything else is exactly the same. Let’s see an example.
